questions.prompt: How is the a in 'Anor' pronounced?

explanation: Elvish vowels have the 'pure' values they have in Italian or Spanish. A is an open 'ah', never the 'ay' of English 'late'.

questions.prompt: How is the first e in 'Elendil' pronounced?

explanation: E is a pure 'eh' sound, never the 'ee' of English 'see'.

questions.prompt: How is the i in 'Ithil' pronounced?
questions.answer: like the i in 'machine', but short

explanation: I is always an 'ee'-type sound, short or long, never the 'eye' of English 'fine'.

questions.prompt: How is the o in 'Mordor' pronounced?
distractors: like the o in 'go', gliding into a 'w'

explanation: O is a pure 'o' with no glide at the end, unlike English 'go' (which ends in a 'w' sound).

questions.prompt: How is the u in 'Isildur' pronounced?
questions.answer: like the u in 'rude', but short

explanation: U is always an 'oo'-type sound, never the 'uh' of 'cut' or the 'you' of 'cute'.

questions.prompt: What does the accent mark in 'Andúril' tell you?
distractors: the vowel is said with a higher pitch

questions.prompt: Which vowel is long in 'Lothlórien'?

explanation: An acute accent (á, é, í, ó, ú) marks a long vowel: the same sound, held for longer.

questions.prompt: In Sindarin, what does the circumflex on the û of 'Lhûn' show?
questions.answer: an extra-long vowel in a one-syllable word

explanation: In Sindarin, a long vowel in a stressed word of one syllable gets a circumflex (â, ê, î, ô, û) instead of an acute accent. It signals a vowel held even longer than usual.

questions.prompt: Is the final e of 'Namárië' pronounced?
questions.answer: yes, a final e is always pronounced
distractors: no, it is silent as in English 'make'
only when the word is sung

explanation: Elvish has no silent letters at the end of words. A final e is a full vowel and makes its own syllable.

questions.prompt: What do the two dots in 'Eärendil' tell you?
questions.answer: e and a are said separately, in two syllables

explanation: The two dots (diaeresis) are only a reading aid: they show that the vowel is pronounced on its own, not merged with its neighbour and not silent.

questions.prompt: How is the ai in 'Dúnedain' pronounced?

explanation: AI is a single gliding sound, like English 'eye' or the 'igh' in 'high'.

questions.prompt: How is the au in 'Rauros' pronounced?

explanation: AU glides from 'a' to 'u', like the 'ow' of 'cow' or the 'ou' of 'house'.

questions.prompt: How is the ui in 'Anduin' pronounced?

explanation: UI is one syllable: start on 'oo' and slide quickly to 'ee', without a break between them.

questions.prompt: How is the ae in 'Gilraen' pronounced?

explanation: In Sindarin, AE is the vowels a and e run together into one syllable.

questions.prompt: How is the y in 'Emyn Muil' pronounced?

explanation: In Sindarin, Y is a vowel: say 'ee' with your lips rounded as for 'oo'. It is never the English 'y' of 'yes' or 'my'.

questions.prompt: How is the c in 'Celeborn' pronounced?

explanation: C is always a hard 'k', even before e and i. Celeborn sounds like 'Keleborn'.

questions.prompt: How is the g in 'Gilraen' pronounced?

explanation: G is always hard, as in 'give' or 'get', never the soft 'j' sound of 'gem'.

questions.prompt: How is the s in 'Isildur' pronounced?

explanation: S is always the hissing 's' of 'so', never the buzzing 'z' that English often uses between vowels.

questions.prompt: How is the th in 'Ithil' pronounced?
distractors: like a t followed by an h

explanation: TH is the breathy, voiceless sound at the start of 'think' and the end of 'bath'.

questions.prompt: How is the dh in 'Caradhras' pronounced?
distractors: like a d followed by an h

explanation: DH is the buzzing, voiced 'th' of 'this' and 'breathe'. Sindarin writes it differently from TH because they are different sounds.

questions.prompt: How is the ch in 'echant' pronounced?
questions.answer: like the ch in German 'Bach' or Scottish 'loch'

explanation: CH is a rasping sound made at the back of the mouth, as in German 'Bach'. It is never the 'ch' of 'church'.

questions.prompt: How is the r in 'Rauros' pronounced?
questions.answer: trilled, with the tip of the tongue

explanation: R is trilled (rolled) wherever it appears, including at the end of a word.

questions.prompt: How is the lh in 'Lhûn' pronounced?
questions.answer: as a breathy l, with air but no voice
distractors: as an l followed by an h

explanation: At the start of a word, LH and RH stand for 'whispered' versions of l and r: air flows but the voice is off.

sound: v at the end of a word

questions.prompt: How is the final f in 'Nindalf' pronounced?

explanation: In Sindarin, F at the end of a word stands for a v sound, as at the end of English 'have'. Elsewhere it is an ordinary f.

questions.prompt: How is the ll in 'mellon' pronounced?
questions.answer: as a long l, held for longer

questions.prompt: In 'Annúminas', what does the double n mean?
distractors: the n is nasal, as in French

explanation: A consonant written twice is pronounced long: you hold it a moment, as in English 'unnamed' or Italian 'nonno'.

questions.prompt: In a word of two syllables, which syllable is usually stressed?

explanation: Two-syllable words are stressed on the first syllable in nearly every case: ITH-il, AR-wen.

questions.prompt: In a longer word, when is the next-to-last syllable stressed?
questions.answer: when it is 'heavy': a long vowel, a diphthong, or a vowel before two consonants
distractors: only when it has an accent mark

questions.prompt: If the next-to-last syllable is 'light' (a short vowel and at most one consonant), where does the stress go?
questions.answer: on the syllable before it, third from the end

explanation: In words of three or more syllables, look at the next-to-last syllable. If it is heavy, it takes the stress; if it is light, the stress moves one syllable further back.
Two syllables, so the first is stressed: I-thil.
The next-to-last syllable has a long vowel (ú), so it takes the stress: an-DÚ-ril.
The next-to-last syllable has a short i followed by two consonants (l, d), so it is heavy and stressed: i-SIL-dur.
The e of the next-to-last syllable is followed by two consonants (n, d), so it is stressed: e-LEN-dil.
The next-to-last syllable (va) is light, so the stress moves back one: i-LÚ-va-tar.
The next-to-last syllable (le) has a short e and only one consonant after it, so the stress moves back: CE-le-born (and remember, 'Ke-').
The double s makes the next-to-last syllable heavy, so it is stressed: e-LES-sar.
